prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Like nights we knelt on the dirt floor of a dugout, leaned our heads back, eyes twitching gone, and popped nitrous canisters into the communion shapes of our mouths, slipped inside where everything seemed to be falling snow, ice, the time split between chasing flies through a darkened park and sprawling in sycamore bark—how clean that abyss we drifted in, like dew, more like pollen, on our skins; and, beneath, a want for touch, a kiss, a return. Like nothing back then, to break an arm latching on to the bumper of an Impala, or settling back as the car took us as far as the salted bridge, before letting the ride go with a mitten caught behind the chrome waving from the other side of the river. Like this, you said, sliding a needle, watching dope plunge, the body's rush and tow until you felt something like an angel hovering above, but it was only pigeon feathers deviling the air. Those friends are gone: some dead, dying, locked up or jailed in themselves; and when I see some kids running in the heat of a taillight swirling behind them, I remember we wanted only to quiet our bodies, their unnatural hum, a vague pull inward, some thin furrows gliding over the snow.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Like, Impala, Those

outputs.L1:
On nights like those, we knelt on the dirt floor of a dugout, leaned our heads back, our eyes twitching, gone, and popped nitrous canisters into the communion shapes of our mouths. We slipped inside, where everything seemed to be falling—snow, ice, time—divided between chasing flies through a darkened park and sprawling against sycamore bark. How clean the abyss we drifted through, like dew—or, more precisely, pollen—on our skin; and beneath it, a longing for touch, a kiss, a return.

Back then, it seemed like nothing to break an arm while clinging to the bumper of an Impala, or to settle back as the car carried us as far as the salted bridge before we let go, a mitten caught behind the chrome, waving from the other side of the river. Like this, you said, sliding in a needle, watching the dope plunge—the body’s rush and pull—until you felt something like an angel hovering above, though it was only pigeon feathers deviling the air.

Those friends are gone: some dead, some dying, some locked up or jailed within themselves. And when I see kids running in the heat of a taillight swirling behind them, I remember that we wanted only to quiet our bodies—their unnatural hum, a vague pull inward, thin furrows gliding over the snow.
outputs.L2: At night, we would drop to our knees on the earthen floor of the dugout, tip back our heads until our eyes fluttered out of sight, and press nitrous cartridges to mouths shaped as if receiving communion. Then we entered a place where all things resembled falling snow and ice, where time divided itself between pursuing flies across an unlit park and lying spread against sycamore bark. The void carrying us felt pure—dewlike, or, more precisely, like pollen dusting our skin—while underneath lingered a craving to be touched, kissed, brought back. In those days, breaking an arm while gripping the bumper of an Impala seemed ordinary. We would let the car drag us to the salt-covered bridge, then release it, leaving a mitten snagged behind the chrome to wave from across the river. This is how, you said, as you pushed in the needle and watched the dope descend: the body surged and was pulled along until something resembling an angel appeared to hover overhead, though it was merely pigeon feathers tormenting the air. Those friends have disappeared—dead, near death, imprisoned, or trapped within themselves. Now, whenever I see children running with the glow of a taillight curling behind them, I remember that all we had wanted was to silence our bodies and their strange vibration: that indistinct inward tug, like narrow grooves moving across snow.
outputs.L3:
The speaker looks back on a youth shaped by reckless nights and desperate attempts to escape reality. With friends, they inhaled nitrous oxide until the familiar world dissolved into a hazy, dissociative dream. Yet beneath the intoxication lay a more vulnerable need: a longing to be held, to feel connected to someone, and to find a way back to safety and belonging.

Their search for relief soon took increasingly dangerous forms. They chased adrenaline by clinging to a moving car as it sped toward a bridge, treating the risk as both entertainment and an act of defiance. Drug use also intensified, eventually leading to heroin injection. The sudden rush felt almost sacred—angelic, transcendent, and briefly capable of silencing every fear—though that sense of deliverance was only an illusion.

Looking back, the speaker recognizes the devastating consequences of those years. Many members of the group are now dead or dying; others are imprisoned, physically confined, or trapped within their own emotional pain. What remains is the memory of a group of young people united not merely by recklessness, but by a shared desire to quiet the turmoil inside themselves. Their destructive choices were attempts to find peace, affection, and escape, even when the methods they chose carried them further from all three.
outputs.L4:
Memory returns in flashes: the metallic sweetness of nitrous, laughter breaking apart in the dark, a body balanced somewhere it should never have been. We were young enough to mistake danger for freedom. We climbed fences, leaned over ledges, drove too fast, and swallowed whatever promised to carry us beyond ourselves. Every stunt felt like a dare addressed to the world: catch us, stop us, prove that we could still be touched.

The drugs were part of that same hunger. Nitrous offered a few bright seconds in which thought loosened its grip and the noise inside went thin and distant. Heroin promised something deeper—a silence that felt almost tender. It was not death we wanted, or not exactly. We wanted relief. We wanted to step outside the restless machinery of longing, to escape the loneliness of our own bodies and find, however briefly, warmth without consequence.

But consequences gathered quietly around us. Years later, the speaker counts the absences: friends buried before they had learned how to live, friends sealed behind prison walls, friends still breathing but unreachable, their old selves erased by repetition and need. The reckless nights that once seemed radiant now cast long shadows. What looked like rebellion was often desperation; what felt like intimacy was sometimes only shared damage.

Looking back does not produce a simple judgment. The speaker understands why they reached for danger and why they mistook oblivion for peace. Beneath every chemical rush and impossible stunt was an ordinary human plea—to be held, to be released, to feel the mind become quiet. That plea has not disappeared with age. It survives alongside grief, carrying the knowledge that every attempt to silence longing leaves an echo, and that some forms of escape demand more than anyone intends to give.
outputs.L5: Like an impala racing across the open savanna, determination can carry us beyond fear. Those who keep moving forward—even when the path is uncertain—often discover strength they never knew they possessed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about reckless adolescence, drug use, lost friends, and the aching desire for human connection, using surreal winter imagery and long, flowing sentences.
counterfactuals.output:
We were sixteen and winter had mistaken the town for a body it could preserve, sealing the river under a cataract of blue glass, packing the alleys with snow that glowed faintly as television static, while we moved through the long white evenings in borrowed coats, our pockets full of pills, matches, dead phone numbers, and the bright counterfeit courage of children who believed ruin was another word for freedom.

In basements where the pipes knocked like trapped saints, we passed smoke from mouth to mouth as if breath itself were proof of love, as if every chemical star dissolving behind our eyes might guide us home, though none of us knew where home was, only that it was warmer than this, only that someone there would touch our face without asking us to become a story first.

Some friends vanished slowly, thinning into rumors, into unanswered messages, into names our mothers lowered their voices to say, and some were gone all at once, leaving behind a jacket stiff with frost, a scratched record turning in an empty room, a silence so enormous it seemed the moon had fallen through the roof and lay there among the bottles, pale and impossible to lift.

Still, we kept running beneath the black trees, laughing too loudly, our blood full of little engines, while snow rose upward around us like a flock of white moths returning to heaven, and every streetlamp wore a halo it had not earned, and every passing car seemed filled with strangers who might save us if only they stopped, if only we could admit we were not fearless but lonely, not wild but wounded, not trying to die so much as trying to feel a hand close around ours in the dark.

Years later, I dream of those nights as a country under ice, our young faces suspended beneath it, beautiful with hunger, our mouths open around words we never learned to say, and I wake reaching across the cold bed for someone living, someone warm, while outside the snow keeps falling through the sleepless city, covering every footprint but never, never the distance between us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph poem in which a speaker remembers doing nitrous and heroin with friends, clinging to a moving car, and later realizing that many of those friends are now dead, imprisoned, or emotionally lost.
counterfactuals.output: We passed the silver mouth of nitrous beneath a jaundiced moon, chased heroin’s hush through rooms where laughter shook the blinds, and once I clung to the bumper of a moving car, shoes sparking against the avenue, certain the night would never dare to end; now I count those friends like vanished stars—some under stone, some behind steel, some walking free with their eyes locked far away—and hear our younger voices thinning in the distance, wild with borrowed breath, calling my name as if I could still hold on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, dreamlike meditation on addiction and youth. Blend images of snow, pollen, pigeon feathers, taillights, and a river bridge, ending with the narrator watching a younger generation repeat similar risks.
counterfactuals.output:
We were young enough to believe every hunger was a doorway.

That winter, snow sifted through the streetlights like ash from a clean, invisible fire. We stood beneath the river bridge with our collars raised, passing the little bright lie from hand to hand. Above us, cars crossed toward the city, their taillights bleeding red through the iron ribs. Below, the river carried black plates of ice downstream, solemn as unopened letters.

By spring, the gutters filled with pollen and pigeon feathers. Everything pale became a kind of weather: dust on the windowsill, powder on the mirror, morning light on a face that had forgotten sleep. We called it freedom because no one came looking. We called it love because we were afraid to be alone. Our bodies were rooms we kept breaking into.

Some of us vanished gradually—first from school, then from photographs, then from the mouths of friends who grew careful with names. Others stayed and learned the ordinary disguises: clean shirts, steady jobs, apologies polished smooth by repetition. But even years later, certain evenings open inside me. Snow begins falling in July. Pollen glows in the dark. A pigeon lifts from the pavement and leaves one gray feather turning where a boy once knelt, swearing he could stop whenever he wanted.

Now I walk the river bridge at dusk. The water below still looks bottomless, though I know its depth. Traffic moves behind me, taillights smearing into long red wounds.

Under the bridge, a new group gathers—young faces lit by their phones, shoulders touching against the cold. They laugh with the same brave carelessness we wore. One of them cups a flame from the wind. Another watches the road as if expecting rescue.

I want to call down. I want to tell them the dream remembers everyone.

But the river keeps moving, and snow—or pollen, or feathers—drifts between us, and I stand above them, old enough now to recognize the doorway, watching them step through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write literary flash prose about a group of troubled teenagers trying to quiet the unbearable “hum” inside their bodies through drugs, dangerous games, and fleeting physical intimacy. Make the tone nostalgic, mournful, and hallucinatory.
counterfactuals.output:
We called it the hum because none of us had a better word.

It lived behind the ribs, in the hinge of the jaw, beneath the blue rivers of our wrists. At night it grew louder. It tuned itself to the refrigerator’s shudder, the freight trains dragging sparks beyond the football field, the power lines singing over the dead corn. If you pressed your ear to another person’s chest, you could hear it there too—or believed you could—which was almost the same thing.

There were six of us that summer, though memory keeps changing the number.

We stole cough syrup and warm beer from unlocked garages. We swallowed whatever pills had lost their labels. We spun in circles on the water tower catwalk until the town tilted loose from the earth. Once, Mara lay down on the yellow line at two in the morning and made us promise not to move her until headlights appeared. The road held the day’s heat against her back. Moths battered themselves senseless against the streetlamps.

We were cruel in the ceremonial ways of the frightened. We dared one another onto roofs, into storm drains, across the quarry on a fallen pine slick with rain. We held our breath underwater while someone counted too slowly. We put our hands over one another’s mouths and called it trust.

Sometimes the hum softened.

It softened when Mara kissed June beneath the bleachers, both of them laughing afterward as if they had fooled death with a cheap trick. It softened when Eli slept with his head in my lap while the others passed a bottle between them and the sky turned the color of a bruise. It softened when we crowded together in the back seat of a rusted sedan, knees and shoulders touching, each body briefly convincing the others that a body could be shelter.

We wanted closeness without consequence, oblivion without dying. We were young enough to believe those things existed.

The town looked beautiful then, though it wasn’t. The refinery burned its orange crown all night. Empty houses leaned into waist-high weeds. The river carried rainbow skins of oil beneath the bridge. But under the influence of whatever we had taken, every ruined thing became holy: broken glass glittered like constellations; abandoned shopping carts became silver animals grazing in the ditch; our faces in the laundromat windows floated pale and saintly above the spinning clothes.

By August, the hum had learned our names.

It called Mara toward the highway. It called Eli into fights he could not win. It called June home to a father who punched holes in doors and then hung family photographs over them. It called all of us, in different voices, toward the edge of something.

The last night, we went to the quarry with no moon.

Someone had brought a handful of pills, blue as robin eggs. Someone else had brought a flare. We stood above the black water, passing both from hand to hand. Below us, our reflections waited without faces.

Mara lit the flare.

For one impossible minute, the whole quarry bloomed red—the cliffs, the pines, our skinny arms, our frightened eyes. Sparks fell around us like furious stars. We shouted because shouting was the only weapon we had. We shouted our names, obscenities, promises. We shouted into the open mouth of the water.

And beneath it all, inside every one of us, the hum went on.

Years later, I sometimes wake with my teeth aching from it. I lie still beside someone kind, in a quiet house far from the refinery, and listen to the appliances breathe. The past comes back in flashes: Mara on the center line, June’s wet hair, Eli asleep against my thigh, the flare burning down to its white and murderous heart.

I want to tell those children to go home.

But there was no home, not in the sense I mean now.

So in memory they remain at the quarry’s edge, luminous and doomed, touching one another’s shoulders in the red dark—each of them pretending, for the sake of the others, not to tremble.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an experimental prose poem with anaphoric phrases such as “Like nights,” “Like nothing,” and “Like this,” exploring memory, self-destruction, incarceration, death, and the fragile beauty of doomed friendships.
counterfactuals.output:
**Inventory of the Vanishing**

Like nights, we counted the bars by touching them with our foreheads, one cold interval after another, until the cell became a calendar and the calendar forgot our names.

Like nights, memory arrived wearing wet shoes. It tracked the old apartment across the floor: burnt spoons, unpaid bills, a window left open to winter, your laughter breaking its bright teeth against the sink.

Like nothing, we promised to survive.

Like nothing, the promise entered us—small contraband, swallowed before inspection.

Like this, you said, and struck a match in the dark. For one second your face was all cheekbone, bruise, and impossible tenderness. For one second the walls leaned away. Then the flame reached your fingers.

We were talented at ruin. We made instruments of ourselves and played until the strings snapped. We drank the evidence. We mistook the edge for a horizon. Each wound opened like a door, and each door led back to the same locked room.

Like nights, the guards passed with keys jangling at their hips, little metallic weather. Somewhere a man prayed into his mattress. Somewhere another man learned that silence has weight, that it can sit on the chest, that it can finish the job.

Like nothing, you disappeared from the tier.

No thunder. No choir. Breakfast arrived in its plastic tray: pale eggs, bruised fruit, a milk carton stamped with tomorrow’s date.

Like this, death edits: not with a black line, but with a blank space everyone keeps reading.

Years later, I still find you in damaged things—the bent cigarette shared behind intake, the paper bird folded from a disciplinary report, the blue vein of dawn beneath the door. We had so little beauty that every scrap became sacred. Even our doomed friendship, especially that: two matches sheltering each other from the wind, burning down.

Like nights, I remember incorrectly. Your eyes change color. Your last words trade places with mine. The dead are patient with our revisions.

Like nothing, I forgive us.

Like this, I fail.

Like this, I keep the match unlit in my palm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
